title: Amalgam & safe mercury handling
blurb: What amalgam is made of, how to triturate and hand it over, and how to protect yourself and the environment from mercury.
question: You are preparing an amalgam restoration for a lower molar. As you take the capsule out of the amalgamator, you notice it was not fully closed and a few small droplets of liquid mercury are on the worktop. What should you do, and what should you never use to clean it up?

teach.body: Dental amalgam is a silver-grey filling material made by mixing an alloy powder (mainly silver, tin and copper) with liquid mercury. Roughly half of a set amalgam is mercury by weight. It is strong, hard-wearing, relatively tolerant of moisture and inexpensive, so it has long been used for posterior fillings. Its downsides are its colour, the fact that it does not bond to the tooth, its high thermal conductivity and the mercury it contains.

rows.label: Handling
values: Must be carved before it sets

rows.label: Cost and heat
values: Conducts heat: may need a lining

items: Use a pre-dosed capsule of the size the dentist asks for (single, double or triple spill). Since 2019 the law allows amalgam only in pre-dosed capsules: bulk mercury is banned.
Activate the capsule if required, place it in the amalgamator, close the lid and triturate for the manufacturer's time.
Empty the mix into an amalgam well or dappens pot and load the amalgam carrier.
Pass the carrier, then the condenser (plugger) to pack the amalgam firmly into the cavity, removing excess mercury.
Pass the carvers to shape the anatomy before it sets, then the burnisher to smooth the margins.
Clear the carrier straight away. Set amalgam left inside will block the barrel.

teach.caption: Use the capsule size the dentist asks for (single, double or triple spill). A glass slab and spatula are for hand-mixed cements, never for amalgam.

teach.body: A well-triturated amalgam is smooth, shiny and plastic. A dry, crumbly mix has been under-triturated or wrongly proportioned and will not condense properly. A very soft, wet or hot mix has usually been over-triturated and will set too fast. Amalgam reaches its full strength over several hours, so the patient should avoid chewing hard on the new filling for the rest of the day. Polishing, if the dentist wants it, is done at a later visit once it has fully set.

items.label: Serious health hazard
items.sub: Repeated exposure harms nerves and kidneys

items.label: Environmental hazard
items.sub: Toxic to aquatic life; never down the drain

teach.caption: The main route into the body is breathing in mercury vapour, which is invisible and has no smell. Heat increases the vapour given off.

rows.label: Encapsulated amalgam only, amalgamator lid closed
Well-ventilated surgery with smooth, sealed flooring (no carpet)
High-volume suction and water spray when old amalgam is drilled out
Remove amalgam debris before instruments go into the washer-disinfector or steriliser
Touch mercury or amalgam with bare hands
Heat amalgam or put it in the clinical waste

teach.note: Wear gloves, mask and eye protection whenever you handle amalgam.

teach.h: Dealing with a small mercury spill

steps.label: Keep people away
steps.sub: Move patients and staff out of the area; don't walk it around

steps.label: Ventilate and put on PPE
steps.sub: Open windows; gloves, mask, eye protection

steps.label: Use the mercury spillage kit
steps.sub: Collect droplets as the kit directs. Never a vacuum cleaner or the surgery suction

steps.label: Seal and label
steps.sub: Into a sealed container for hazardous amalgam waste

steps.label: Record and report
steps.sub: Tell the practice manager; follow the COSHH procedure

teach.caption: A vacuum cleaner or aspirator spreads the mercury and turns it into vapour. A large spill needs specialist help.

teach.body: Amalgam waste is hazardous waste. Waste amalgam, used capsules and extracted teeth containing amalgam go into a sealed, labelled white container with a mercury vapour suppressant, collected by a licensed contractor with a consignment note. The EU Mercury Regulation (2017/852), kept in GB law after Brexit, sets the rules. Practices using or removing amalgam must have an amalgam separator that retains at least 95% of amalgam particles, so mercury does not reach the drains. Amalgam may only be used in pre-dosed capsules. Since July 2018 it should not be used for deciduous teeth, children under 15, or pregnant or breastfeeding women, unless the dentist judges it strictly necessary for the patient's specific medical needs.

teach.text: Amalgam waste does NOT go in the yellow or orange clinical waste bags or the sharps bin. It goes in its own white container with mercury vapour suppressant, and that includes teeth with amalgam fillings.

items: Amalgam = alloy powder (silver, tin, copper) + mercury, supplied in pre-dosed capsules.
Triturate in an amalgamator; dry and crumbly means under-triturated or wrongly proportioned.
Condense, carve before it sets, burnish; full strength takes hours.
Mercury vapour is the main hazard: ventilate, use spillage kits, never vacuum.
Waste in a white container with vapour suppressant; separators trap particles in the suction.

summary: You can now describe what amalgam is made of, prepare and hand over the instruments in order, recognise a poor mix, explain why the patient avoids chewing hard on it that day, keep yourself safe from mercury vapour, deal with a small spill and dispose of amalgam waste correctly under UK rules.

A.q: Straight after trituration, the amalgam mix looks dry and crumbly. What is the most likely cause?
options: It was under-mixed or wrongly proportioned
The capsule held too much mercury
Saliva got into the capsule during mixing
A.why: A dry, crumbly mix has not been mixed for long enough or has the wrong proportions, so it won't condense properly.

whyNot.0: Over-trituration gives a soft, wet, hot mix that sets too quickly.
whyNot.2: Excess mercury would make the mix wetter, not dry and crumbly.
whyNot.3: The capsule is sealed during trituration, so saliva can't get in while it mixes.

A.q: A few droplets of mercury have been spilled on the surgery floor. Which action is WRONG?
A.why: A vacuum cleaner spreads mercury droplets and turns them into vapour, increasing everyone's exposure.

whyNot.0: Ventilation reduces the concentration of mercury vapour in the air.
whyNot.1: PPE protects you while you deal with the spill.
whyNot.2: The spillage kit is the correct way to collect and contain the mercury.

A.q: Where should waste amalgam from a restoration be placed?
options: A sealed white amalgam waste container
A.why: Amalgam is hazardous waste and goes in a sealed, labelled white container with a mercury vapour suppressant.

whyNot.0: The yellow-lidded sharps bin is for medicinally contaminated sharps, not amalgam.
whyNot.1: Orange bags are for infectious waste sent for alternative treatment, which could release mercury.
whyNot.3: Tiger-striped bags are for non-infectious offensive waste like couch roll.

B.q: A patient asks why they shouldn't chew hard on their new amalgam filling today. What is the best explanation?
options: It takes several hours to reach full strength
Chewing would release mercury from its surface
Its silver colour hasn't fully developed yet
The anaesthetic keeps the filling soft for now
B.why: Amalgam keeps hardening for hours after it is placed, so heavy biting too soon could fracture it.

whyNot.1: Chewing on a new filling isn't the reason for this advice; strength is.
whyNot.2: Amalgam's colour doesn't change as it sets.
whyNot.3: Local anaesthetic numbs the tissues; it has no effect on the filling material.

B.q: What is the main route by which dental staff could absorb mercury from amalgam?
B.why: Mercury vapour is invisible and odourless, and inhaling it is the main occupational risk. Heat makes more vapour.

whyNot.0: Staff don't swallow amalgam; ingestion is not the main occupational route.
whyNot.2: A set restoration releases very little mercury on touch, although you should always wear gloves.
whyNot.3: The curing light is used for resin materials and has nothing to do with mercury.

B.q: What is the purpose of an amalgam separator?
options: To separate alloy powder from mercury
To remove excess mercury from the mix
To trap amalgam particles in the suction
B.why: The separator traps amalgam particles from the suction system so mercury does not reach the drains. It must retain at least 95% of particles.

whyNot.0: Capsules keep powder and mercury apart until trituration; that's not a separator's job.
whyNot.1: Excess mercury is removed during condensation, not by the separator.
whyNot.3: Capsules are stored in their packaging; separators are part of the suction system.

C.q: At the end of a session, the amalgam carrier won't eject. What is the most likely reason?
options: It has been sterilised too many times
Set amalgam was left inside the barrel
Saliva has corroded the inner barrel
It was used with the wrong type of alloy
C.why: Amalgam left in the carrier sets hard and blocks it, so the carrier should be cleared straight after use.

whyNot.0: Routine sterilisation doesn't block a carrier.
whyNot.2: Carriers are made to tolerate saliva; corrosion isn't the usual cause.
whyNot.3: Any amalgam left inside will set and block it, whatever the alloy.

C.q: Why must amalgam be carved before it sets?
options: Carving helps it bond to enamel
Carving makes it set more slowly
Set amalgam is too hard to shape
C.why: Once amalgam has set, it is too hard to carve with hand instruments, so the anatomy must be shaped while it is still workable.

whyNot.0: Excess mercury is removed by condensing, not carving.
whyNot.1: Amalgam does not bond to enamel; it is held by the cavity shape.
whyNot.2: Carving doesn't change the setting reaction.

C.q: Which of these patients should NOT normally have amalgam placed under UK rules?
C.why: Since July 2018, amalgam should not be used for pregnant or breastfeeding women, children under 15 or deciduous teeth, unless strictly necessary for medical reasons.

whyNot.0: Adults who are not pregnant or breastfeeding are not covered by the restriction.
whyNot.1: The age restriction applies to children under 15, so a 16-year-old is not covered.
whyNot.2: Older adults are not covered by the restriction.

reteach.title: Treat mercury like an invisible gas leak
reteach.question: You can't see or smell mercury vapour, just like some gas leaks. How does that change the way you work with amalgam?

blocks.body: Liquid mercury gives off vapour at room temperature, and warmth makes it give off more. You can't see it or smell it, so you rely on habits: keep amalgam sealed in capsules, keep the room ventilated, never heat it, and never stir up a spill with a vacuum cleaner. Treat every bit of amalgam as hazardous until it is sealed in its white waste pot.

children.label: Excess mix and used capsules
children.sub: White amalgam waste pot with vapour suppressant

blocks.text: Never put amalgam in clinical waste for incineration or treatment: heating it releases mercury vapour into the air.

explain.body: Amalgam is an alloy powder of mainly silver, tin and copper mixed with liquid mercury. It must now be supplied in pre-dosed capsules, which keep the powder and mercury apart until the capsule is activated and triturated in an amalgamator.

test.q: What is the liquid component of dental amalgam?
test.why: Amalgam is made by mixing alloy powder with liquid mercury.

whyNot.0: Phosphoric acid is the liquid of zinc phosphate cement and the acid in etchant.
whyNot.2: Eugenol is the liquid of zinc oxide eugenol.
whyNot.3: Polyacrylic acid is the liquid of glass ionomer and polycarboxylate cements.

explain.body: The carrier takes amalgam to the cavity, condensers pack it in and squeeze out excess mercury, carvers shape it before it sets, and the burnisher smooths the margins. Clear the carrier straight away, and remind the patient to avoid chewing hard on it today.

test.q: Which instrument is used to pack amalgam firmly into the cavity?
test.why: The condenser (plugger) packs amalgam into the cavity and brings excess mercury to the surface.

whyNot.0: The burnisher smooths the surface and margins after carving.
whyNot.1: Carvers shape the anatomy after condensing.
whyNot.3: An excavator removes soft caries before the filling is placed.

explain.body: Mercury vapour is the hazard. Work in a ventilated room with sealed flooring, use capsules, close the amalgamator lid, use high-volume suction when removing old amalgam, and keep a mercury spillage kit. Never vacuum a spill or heat amalgam.

test.q: Which flooring is most suitable for a surgery where amalgam is used?
test.why: Smooth, sealed flooring with coved edges has no gaps where mercury droplets can collect, and it is easy to clean.

whyNot.0: Carpet traps mercury droplets and can't be decontaminated properly.
whyNot.1: Gaps and grain in untreated boards trap droplets.
whyNot.3: Gaps in matting trap droplets and are hard to clean.

explain.body: Amalgam waste goes in a sealed white container with mercury vapour suppressant, collected by a licensed contractor. Separators trap at least 95% of amalgam particles from the suction. Since July 2018, amalgam should not be used for deciduous teeth, under-15s or pregnant or breastfeeding women unless the dentist judges it strictly necessary.

items.label: White container
items.sub: Dental amalgam, with mercury vapour suppressant

test.q: A tooth with a large amalgam filling has just been extracted. How should it be disposed of?
options: In the orange clinical waste bag
In the red anatomical waste bin
test.why: Teeth containing amalgam go into the amalgam waste stream so the mercury is not incinerated or released.

whyNot.1: The sharps bin is incinerated, which would release mercury from the filling.
whyNot.2: Orange waste goes for treatment that isn't designed for mercury.
whyNot.3: Red anatomical waste is incinerated and isn't the stream for amalgam-filled teeth.
